equipment: Digital scale accurate to at least 0.1 g (0.01 g ideal for preservatives)
Immersion (stick) blender - a whisk alone cannot form a stable emulsion
Two heat-proof glass beakers or funnel pitchers (one for the water phase, one for the oil phase)
Large pot or skillet with 2-3 cm of water plus a wire rack or canning ring, to act as a double boiler / water bath
Spray bottle of 70% isopropyl alcohol for sanitizing
Flexible spatulas and pipettes for cool-down ingredients
Disposable piping bag or zip-top bag for filling bottles cleanly
Final packaging: pump, disc-cap, or flip-top bottles preferred over open jars
Stovetop or portable burner, timer, and paper towels
safety: This is the golden rule from every authority (Soap Queen, Humblebee & Me, School of Natural Skincare, Wholesale Supplies Plus): ANY product containing water - lotion, cream, anything with hydrosols, aloe, or milks - MUST contain a broad-spectrum preservative. Unpreserved lotion can grow mold and bacteria within days to weeks, sometimes invisibly.

Anhydrous whipped body butters and balms (100% oils, butters, waxes) do not support microbial growth and do not require a preservative - but add an antioxidant like vitamin E to delay rancidity, and add a preservative anyway if the product will be scooped with wet fingers or stored in a steamy bathroom.
Sanitize the workspace, every tool, and every container with 70% isopropyl alcohol before starting; work with gloves and tied-back hair.
Use distilled or deionized water only - never tap water, which carries minerals and microbes.
Heat-and-hold both phases at 158°F (70°C) for 20 minutes to kill microbes in the raw ingredients and ensure full emulsifier melt.

Respect preservative parameters: Liquid Germall Plus at 0.5% (max - more is not better), Germaben II at 1%, Optiphen at 1.5%, all added in cool-down below about 104-115°F; check each preservative's pH range and incompatibilities (e.g., Optiphen ND conflicts with BTMS-50).
Hot oil and water phases scald - use pot holders, keep beaker handles inward, and never blend hot liquid in an overfilled container.
Label with an ingredient declaration and follow FDA cosmetic labeling rules if the product leaves your house.

phases.title: Phase 1 - Sanitize and weigh the phases
steps: Spray your counter, beakers, spatulas, immersion blender head, and bottles with 70% isopropyl alcohol and let them air-dry.

Write your formula in percentages totaling 100, then convert to grams for your batch size. A proven beginner structure (cross-referencing Wholesale Supplies Plus and Soap Queen): water phase 70-80% (distilled water, plus 2-5% humectant such as glycerin or sodium lactate); oil phase 15-25% (oils and butters 10-20%, emulsifying wax 3-6%, optional stearic acid 2% as thickener); cool-down 2-3% (preservative about 1% and fragrance up to 2%).

A concrete example - WSP's Basic Body Lotion: 64% distilled water, 3% glycerin, 2% sodium lactate, 16% avocado oil, 5% shea butter, 5% emulsifying wax, 2% stearic acid, 2% fragrance, 1% Germaben II. Humblebee & Me's beginner version: 74% distilled water, 5% sodium lactate, 5% Ritamulse SCG, 15% MCT oil, 1% preservative.
Weigh the water phase ingredients into one heat-proof beaker and the oil phase ingredients (including the emulsifying wax - it always goes in the oil phase) into the other.
Weigh out the cool-down ingredients into small cups and set them aside where they will not be knocked over.

phases.title: Phase 2 - Heat and hold both phases (158°F / 70°C for 20 minutes)
steps: Bring 2-3 cm (about 1 inch) of water to a bare simmer in the pot and place both beakers in this water bath on the wire rack.

Heat both phases to 158°F (70°C), checking with the thermometer, and hold them there for a full 20 minutes - this pasteurizes the ingredients and guarantees the emulsifying wax and butters are completely melted.
Stir each phase occasionally with its own clean spatula; the oil phase is ready only when it is fully transparent liquid with no waxy flecks.
Top up the water phase with a splash of extra distilled water if noticeable evaporation occurs during the hold (some makers pre-weigh about 10% extra water to compensate).

Make sure both phases are at the same temperature (within a few degrees of each other, around 158°F) before combining - combining phases at mismatched temperatures is a classic cause of failed, separated emulsions.

phases.title: Phase 3 - Combine and emulsify
steps: Remove both beakers from the water bath and slowly pour the water phase into the oil phase (or oil into water - consistency matters less than temperature) while stirring.

Immediately blend with the immersion blender in short bursts, keeping the head fully submerged to avoid whipping in air; the mixture will quickly turn opaque, milky white - that color change is the emulsion forming.
Blend for 1-2 minutes, rest, then blend again in short bursts every few minutes as the lotion cools; it will visibly thicken as the temperature drops.
Be patient: lotion reaches most of its thickness as it cools, and full final viscosity only after about 24 hours - do not add more emulsifier just because the warm mixture looks thin.

phases.title: Phase 4 - Cool-down additions (below 104-115°F / 40-45°C)
steps: Let the emulsion cool, stirring occasionally, until it is below about 104°F / 40°C (Humblebee & Me's threshold; WSP uses below 115°F / 45°C) - if you have no thermometer, the beaker should feel only slightly warm, like bath water.

Add the preservative at its correct rate (e.g., Liquid Germall Plus 0.5%, Germaben II 1%, or Optiphen 1.5%) and stir or briefly blend until fully incorporated - adding it hotter than its tolerance degrades it and silently leaves the lotion unprotected.
Add fragrance or essential oil (typically up to 1-2% for body products) and any other heat-sensitive extracts or actives.
Keep the entire cool-down phase to 10% or less of the formula - per Humblebee & Me, dumping too much into an already-formed emulsion can destabilize it.
Give one final short blend so everything is uniform.

phases.title: Phase 5 - Bottle, cure, and label
steps: Spoon or pipe the finished lotion into sanitized bottles using a piping bag or zip-top bag with a corner snipped off, filling from the bottom up to avoid air pockets.

Cap immediately; pump, disc-cap, and flip-top bottles are strongly preferred over open jars because every open-jar scoop introduces air and skin flora (if you must use a jar, use the preservative at its maximum recommended rate).
Wipe bottles clean, then let the lotion sit 24 hours to reach final thickness before judging or adjusting the formula.
Label with product identity, net weight in ounces and grams, business name and address, and the full INCI ingredient list in descending order of predominance.
Date each batch and keep a batch log (formula, lot numbers, date) so any problem can be traced.

finishing: Store finished lotion in a cool, dark place away from direct sunlight and heat; heat stresses both the emulsion and the preservative.
A properly preserved lotion in clean packaging is typically good for about 1 year, but never longer than the earliest expiry/rancidity date of the oils used in it.
Watch for spoilage signs at every use: separation, off or sour smell, color change, or any fuzzy growth means discard the whole container immediately - and remember contamination is often invisible.

For anhydrous whipped butters: store below about 75°F so they do not melt and lose their whip, no preservative needed if kept dry, and expect roughly a 6-12 month life driven by the oils' freshness (add 0.5% vitamin E to extend it).
If selling, consider basic challenge/microbial testing (home microbial test kits exist, e.g., from Lotion Crafter) before scaling up a new formula.
tips: Formulate in percentages and weigh everything - it makes batches reproducible, scalable, and lets you dose the preservative correctly every time.
More water = thinner lotion; more oils/butters/e-wax = thicker cream. Adjust texture by moving 2-5% between the water and oil phases rather than rewriting the whole formula.

Match the emulsifier to its documented usage rate: Polawax/e-wax NF at 3-6% of total weight (a common rule of thumb is about 25% of the oil phase), BTMS-50 at 1-15% for a conditioning powder-soft feel, Ritamulse SCG at about 1% per 4-5% of oil (max ~25% oil phase) for a natural-certified option.
Fix a separated batch by reheating both it and a little extra emulsifier gently to about 130°F and re-blending - hotter than that risks degrading the preservative already in it.
Germall Plus is the closest thing to a foolproof beginner preservative: broad pH range, water-soluble, hard to deactivate, used at just 0.5%.
mistakes: Skipping the preservative or substituting a non-preservative (vitamin E, grapefruit seed extract, 'natural antibacterials') in a water-containing product - antioxidants slow rancidity but do nothing against bacteria and mold, and unpreserved lotion can be growing pathogens within weeks even while it still looks fine.
Skipping heat-and-hold or combining phases at very different temperatures, which produces an emulsion that splits hours or days later.
Adding preservative or fragrance while the emulsion is still hot (above roughly 104-115°F), which degrades them - the lotion smells weak and, worse, is no longer reliably preserved.
Using tap water, unsanitized tools, or double-dipped fingers, seeding the product with microbes the preservative then has to fight from day one.
Judging thickness too early and over-correcting with extra emulsifying wax - lotion thickens dramatically as it cools over 24 hours, and overloaded e-wax gives a heavy, soapy, draggy skin feel.
